131.quote_or_event: Rājīmatī to the monk Rathanemi, who tried to seduce her: “Fie upon you, famous knight, who want to quaff the vomited drink for the sake of this life; it would be better for you to die.”
131.explanation: Rājīmatī, true to her vows, tells a lapsing monk that death is preferable to breaking his conduct, and her words turn him back to the Law; the verse also recurs in the Daśavaikālika (2.7).
131.tie_back: Valluvar says conduct must be guarded above life itself, and Rājīmatī states that rule in its starkest form: better to die than fall from one's vows.
131.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 22.40–46, quoting 22.42 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
131._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi notes the Daśavaikālika parallel); a strong fit for conduct ranked above life, set in an ascetic rather than general context.

132.quote_or_event: “Neither his kinsmen, nor his friends, nor his sons, nor his relations will share his suffering, he alone has to bear it; for the Karman follows the doer. Leaving behind bipeds and quadrupeds, his fields, his house, his wealth, his corn, and everything; against his will, and accompanied only by his Karman, he enters a new existence, either a good or a bad one.”
132.explanation: The sage Citra tells King Brahmadatta that at death everything is left behind and only one's karma, the fruit of one's conduct, goes along.
132.tie_back: Valluvar finds after weighing everything that conduct alone is the companion that stays; Citra's sermon makes karma, the fruit of conduct, the only thing that goes with a person into the next life.
132._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a close fit, though the Jain text speaks of karma (good or bad) as the companion, not specifically of good conduct.

133.quote_or_event: “The value of penance has become visible, birth appears of no value! Look at the holy Harikêśa, the son of a Śvapâka, whose power is so great.”
133.explanation: Harikeśa-Bala, born among the Śvapākas (outcastes) and mocked by priests 'stuck up by pride of birth', is honoured by gods for his discipline, and the scene ends with this verdict.
133.tie_back: Valluvar says conduct is what makes birth noble and its lack makes it low; the Jain canon dramatizes the same reversal, with an outcaste's conduct outranking the priests' high birth.
133.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.1, 12.5 and 12.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
133._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong match on conduct over birth, though the text speaks of penance (tapas) as the measure.

134.quote_or_event: “Those who are full of anger and pride, who kill, lie, steal, and own property, are Brâhmaṇas without pure birth and knowledge; they are very bad fields. You are only the bearer of words as it were, you do not understand their meaning, though you have learned the Vêdas.”
134.explanation: Answering Brahmin priests who claim to be the best recipients by pure birth and learning, the Jain monk says that their misconduct has already destroyed both their birth and their knowledge.
134.tie_back: Valluvar says a Brahmin who forgets the Vedas can learn them again, but one who falls from conduct ruins his birth; this passage likewise says that conduct, not Vedic learning, decides whether a Brahmin's birth counts as pure.
134._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; close match on birth and Vedic learning made worthless by misconduct, framed as a Jain critique of Brahmin claims rather than the Kural's affirmation of Brahmin duty.

135.quote_or_event: “Men who adhering to wrong principles acquire wealth by evil deeds, will lose it, falling into the snares (of their passions) and being held captive by their hatred.”
135.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana teaches that prosperity won through wrong conduct does not last, because the passions that produced it also undo it.
135.tie_back: The Kural says that, as prosperity never settles on the envious, so eminence never comes to one without conduct; this verse makes the related point that gains without right conduct do not endure.
135._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; only a partial match: it covers prosperity lost through misconduct and passion but says nothing specifically about envy (azhukkaaru).

136.quote_or_event: “Though others sleep, be thou awake! Like a wise man, trust nobody, but be always on the alert; for dangerous is the time and weak the body. Be always watchful like a Bhâruṇḍa bird!”
136.explanation: Mahāvīra urges constant vigilance (apramāda), because the monk knows how dangerous time is and how easily one falls.
136.tie_back: Valluvar's strong-minded never slacken in conduct because they know the harm a lapse brings; the Jain call to unsleeping watchfulness rests on the same clear sight of danger.
136._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a close fit on unrelenting vigilance grounded in awareness of danger.

137.quote_or_event: “As a bitch with sore ears is driven away everywhere, thus a bad, insubordinate, and talkative (pupil) is turned out. … Hearing a man thus compared to a dog and a pig, he who desires his own welfare, should adhere to good conduct.”
137.explanation: The lecture on discipline contrasts the disgrace of the ill-behaved, who are driven out everywhere, with the honour of those who follow the conduct of the wise and 'will not incur blame' (1.42).
137.tie_back: The Kural pairs greatness gained by conduct with needless disgrace earned by lapse; the Uttarādhyayana draws the same contrast in social terms of expulsion versus honour.
137._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a good fit on the public honour or disgrace that follows conduct, though set in the teacher–pupil context.

138.quote_or_event: “As the burglar caught in the breach of the wall perishes by the work the sinner himself had executed, thus people in this life and the next cannot escape the effect of their own actions.”
138.explanation: The Jain doctrine of karma holds that deeds bind subtle matter to the soul and ripen into their own results in this life and later ones.
138.tie_back: Valluvar calls good conduct the seed of good and bad conduct a constant source of sorrow; the burglar crushed by his own tunnel is the Jain image of misconduct bearing its own painful fruit.
138._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; fits the causal 'harvest' of conduct well but stresses only the bad side, not good conduct as a seed.

139.quote_or_event: “A monk should avoid untruth, nor should he speak positively (about future things, his plans, &c.); he should avoid sinful speech, and always keep free from deceit. He should not tell anything sinful or meaningless or hurtful, neither for his own sake nor for anybody else's, nor without such a motive.”
139.explanation: The disciplined monk avoids harmful speech whatever the circumstances, even when he has no motive at all.
139.tie_back: Valluvar says people of right conduct cannot utter evil words even by a slip; the Jain rule likewise rules out hurtful speech 'without such a motive', that is, even when it would be idle or unintended.
139._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; matches the prohibition on evil speech, but it is framed as a rule to keep rather than the Kural's claim that the virtuous become incapable of such speech.

140.quote_or_event: “Acknowledging the truth about bondage and liberation, but talking only, not acting (in accordance with these tenets), they seek comfort for themselves in mighty words. Clever talking will not work salvation; how should philosophical instruction do it? Fools, though sinking lower and lower through their sins, believe themselves to be wise men.”
140.explanation: Mahāvīra condemns those who know the doctrine but do not live it, calling them fools who think themselves wise.
140.tie_back: Valluvar says those who have learned much but cannot live in harmony with the world are ignorant; the Jain verse likewise judges learning without matching conduct to be no wisdom at all.
140._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; matches the paradox of the learned fool, but the Kural's criterion of harmony with the world (social fit) differs from the Jain criterion of acting on doctrine.
